title: Angel investing for small startups: add a zero, take more risk, own your audience
summary: Jason explains how profitable "dude businesses" doing about $1M a year can raise angel money to scale, what angels expect, and why founders should take more risk and run cheap experiments. He also covers why he moved Inside.com from apps to email and why podcast networks struggle.

principles.text: Own a direct relationship with your audience; use platforms only for customers, and collect emails everywhere.
principles.quote: I think use any of these other platforms if it gets you customers, but own a direct deep relationship.

principles.text: Taking angel money is a starter pistol: investors expect a return, so deploy it intelligently on growth.
principles.quote: in fact that’s the starter pistol as we talked about earlier. That just means okay, now you’ve deployed it, and those people want you to return.

principles.text: Most founders under-risk. A failed startup makes you more credible, not dead, so take more risk.
principles.quote: if you’re climbing the startup mountain and you fall, it gives you more credibility, and you just get to start over at the bottom of the mountain again.

principles.text: Treat experiments as probes: find the cheapest, quickest way to get a signal, then follow revenue, engagement and open rates.
principles.quote: what’s the least costly and quickest way to get the signal to understand if this is gonna work or not? That’s your goal.

principles.text: Pitch angels in a few sentences: what you do, a revenue chart, and a demo link. Skip the life story.
principles.quote: “I have a business called blank. We make money by doing blank for blank. Here’s a revenue chart, quarterly, monthly, week, whatever, and here’s a link to our product demo.”

principles.text: Send investors a monthly update with metrics. The discipline of writing it plus a clear plan makes companies more successful.
principles.quote: If you have a plan to be successful and you execute the plan, you will be more successful.
